# Introduction

Brazilian agribusiness generates nearly a quarter of the national gross domestic
product and accounts for over 40 percent of national exports
[@basso_agriculture_2024]. Supported by technological intensification and total
factor productivity growth over several decades, national grain production reached
352 million metric tons in the 2024/25 crop year, mainly due to soybean and maize
yields destined for both domestic and international markets [@conab_portal_2026b;
@mascarenhas2014]. However, national static storage capacity remains below 65% of
that volume [@conab_portal_2026a] and logistics depend on a non-optimized network.

Brazil's Artificial Intelligence Plan identifies high-performance computing
infrastructure and technical capacity as priorities for research and innovation
[@mcti2025pbia]. The National Laboratory for Scientific Computing is developing a
separate AI-oriented supercomputing installation in Macaíba, Rio Grande do Norte
[@lncc2026supercomputador]. Research in agricultural operational and logistic
efficiencies are included as priority topics to be addressed from infrastructure
investments [@pera2026]. Embrapa's AgroDigital initiative has acquired
high-performance computing and GPU servers to support research that requires
substantial data processing and storage [@embrapa2024datacenter]. These initiatives
illustrate the importance of high performance computing (HPC) infrastructure across
this research domain.

Grain-storage networks connect seasonal harvests with demand distributed across
places and periods. Choosing where to open or expand warehouses affects how much
grain can be held, how quickly it can be received and dispatched, and which markets
the network can serve. Grain-storage planning raises a specific computational
problem. The selection of warehouse sites and the sizing of storage and handling
capacity combine discrete investment choices with flows that vary across products,
periods and scenarios. A larger network increases the number of decisions and can
place substantial demands on model construction, memory and solution time. This study
uses experiments at an HPC infrastructure to examine the conditions under which
deterministic and two-stage stochastic mixed-integer linear programs yield
optimization plans for soybean and corn storage networks. The analysis relates
measured computation metrics and attainable solution quality to the investment and
strategic decisions that the models return.

Grain-storage location and integrated network design are established research
topics [@essien2018; @gholamian2017]. Agricultural network uncertainty has also
been addressed through wheat-network design and tactical soybean planning
[@hosseini2020; @reis2023]. Decomposition and distributed computing already
provide computational precedents in agricultural MILP [@shastri2011].
The study connects the effort needed to construct and solve these models with
the certified quality and agricultural implications of the plans they return.

Therefore, the research question is: How computational scalability affects the
optimal resolution of grain-storage network design and hub location models?
Optimality is evaluated in terms of MILP solution quality attainable.

The general objective is to investigate the effects of computational scalability in
the resolution of grain-storage network design and hub location models in an HPC
infrastructure. The specific objectives seek three distinct contributions. C1
characterizes observed matrix dimensions, construction and solution effort, memory
and certified gaps across the evaluated populations. C2 interprets the returned
investment and operating decisions by separating financial costs, artificial
penalties, domestic service and capacity exceedances. C3 documents human-supervised
AI assistance and verification as a complementary account of research practice,
detailed in Appendix B. @tbl-objectives links the four specific objectives to the
contributions they support.

| Specific Objective | Scope | Contribution |
|:--|:--|:--|
| SO1 Mathematical modeling | Implement deterministic and two-stage stochastic MILPs for warehouse location, capacity investment and grain-network operation | C1, C2 |
| SO2 Computational scalability | Measure model construction, memory, optimization time, allocated resources and attainable solution quality as warehouse populations increase | C1 |
| SO3 Agricultural interpretation | Interpret validated location, capacity-investment and grain-distribution decisions across h215, h300, h400 and h500 | C2 |
| SO4 Complementary methodology | Document human-supervised AI assistance, scientific decision provenance, verification and reproducibility | C3 |

: Research objectives. {#tbl-objectives}

The next section situates these objectives in agricultural planning and computational
optimization. The methods and results then connect the model, resource measurements
and independently checked solutions to storage-network decisions.

# Related work and research positioning

## Grain-storage planning as an integrated decision problem

The systematic review by @rosa2025 places grain-warehouse location within a broader
family of mathematical planning models. Complementarily, @garima2024 organize grain
supply-chain decision research around operational complexity, risk, infrastructure,
stakeholders and solution methods. Together, these perspectives show why adding sites
to a location model is insufficient: a strategic design must connect storage,
seasonal handling and access to markets. The following synthesis compares published
approaches along these substantive dimensions. [Appendix
A](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/supplementary-review.html)
provides the search strategy, selection record and the complete systematic literature
review.

Integrated wheat-network design in @gholamian2017 links infrastructure choices to the
organization of the supply chain. Scenario-based wheat planning in @pourmohammadi2020
and sustainable resilient network design in @hosseini2020 extend this perspective to
uncertain conditions and competing performance concerns. These contributions motivate
an integrated treatment, but their commodity systems, constraints and objectives
cannot be transferred unchanged to a Brazilian grain-storage network. In particular,
resilience to disruption, seasonal variation and a numerical relaxation of capacity
are different concepts. A slack preserves a mathematical solution; it does not by
itself provide the transport, temporary equipment or institutional arrangements that
would make the physical network resilient.

@essien2018 address stakeholder objectives in grain-storage planning, and
@filippi2022 examine the governance of rural warehouse condominiums. In the
goal-programming model of @essien2018, the number of sites is prescribed and
stakeholder transport targets enter the objective. Here the model sizes
capacity and links investment to scenario-dependent operation. Land access,
financing and operating agreements remain part of the appraisal of any
candidate location.

## Closest precedents and the scope of the empirical question

The closest agricultural studies establish why location and uncertainty alone
cannot define this article's gap. @tbl-closest-precedents distinguishes their
decision or computational emphasis from the assessment undertaken here.
The studies differ in decision horizon, infrastructure choices and solution
method. These distinctions determine which aspects can inform the present
assessment.

| Precedent | Established decision or computational emphasis | Research question examined |
|:--|:--|:--|
| @essien2018 | Multi-stakeholder grain-storage location and decision support | How do returned investment and service outcomes relate to a certified scalar objective? |
| @gholamian2017 | Integrated wheat-network planning, including silo location and distribution | What construction, solution and memory requirements accompany explicitly defined extensive-form instances? |
| @pourmohammadi2020 | Scenario-based location and discrete storage sizing with hard demand fulfillment | How do continuous capacity sizing and penalized shortages change the interpretation of returned plans? |
| @hosseini2020 | Wheat-network design/redesign with sustainability and resilience concerns | What do the present cost and slack variables support, without adding unmodeled resilience or sustainability outcomes? |
| @reis2023 | Two-stage tactical soybean LP with purchasing and transport contracts; 243 scenarios | How does shared infrastructure investment differ from tactical contracting under uncertainty? |
| @shastri2011 | Decomposition and distributed solution of an agricultural MILP | What attainable quality and resource use are observed for the present direct extensive-form solution? |

: Closest agricultural and computational precedents. {#tbl-closest-precedents}

These studies motivate distinct comparisons. Discrete sizing and hard demand
fulfillment in @pourmohammadi2020 clarify how continuous capacity choices and
penalized shortage affect the interpretation of a returned plan. @hosseini2020 treat
sustainability and resilience as modeled concerns. @shastri2011 evaluate
decomposition and distributed solution. This study asks a different planning question
and adds explicit attention to construction, attained integer-solution quality,
computation resorces use and the physical interpretation of the returned capacity
plan for grain-storage strategic decisions.

## Network representation and decision horizons

Dynamic-network models connect storage investment to grain flows over time
[@foulds2005]. In a Brazilian soybean setting, @mascarenhas2014 study warehousing
location with road and intermodal export connections. The distinction is
consequential: a throughput facility that transfers arrivals onward is not
interchangeable with a warehouse that carries inventory between months. Static stock
capacity, annual throughput and vehicle capacity must therefore remain separate
dimensions in a benchmark. The logistics-integration-center formulation of
@guimaraes2017 preserves origin-destination demand relationships. By contrast, the
present model conserves each product but does not retain an origin label after it
enters a warehouse. Product from different origins can satisfy the same customer's
demand. This assumption is appropriate for a fungible-commodity planning abstraction,
but not for tracing contracts, quality lots or individual consignments.

Terminal siting in @morais2023 connects location, capacity choices and access to
railways or waterways. @milanez2026 integrate soybean export network design with hub
functions and economies of scale. One variant permits seaport-capacity overflow at a
penalty, reporting CPU time and optimality gaps. Penalized capacity relief and
computational quality reporting therefore have direct precedents. These studies
motivate reporting storage and transport decisions together. Multimodal models also
represent modal transfers and transport beyond those outlets. The present network
represents road movements to domestic destinations and export ports. @tbl-literature
summarizes the selected agricultural network-design studies, their modeling
distinctions and implications for comparbility.

| Study | Network and decision emphasis | Comparison implication |
|:--|:--|:--|
| @foulds2005 | Dynamic grain-silo location and flow | Separate network size, capacity decisions and temporal flow |
| @mascarenhas2014 | Mato Grosso soybean warehouses and export connections | Distinguish throughput facilities from stock-carrying warehouses |
| @guimaraes2017 | Logistics integration centers and peer-to-peer demand | Commodity mixing differs from origin-destination preservation |
| @morais2023 | Capacitated terminals with intermodal location preferences | Modal access is not equivalent to a road-distance proxy |
| @milanez2026 | Hub location and soybean-export network design | Report hub function, capacity and route use together |
| @granillo2019 | Contract-farming network with simulation and MILP | Simulation-based uncertainty is not automatically two-stage recourse |
| @mendoza2021 | Scenario-based agro-food facility location | State which decisions precede the uncertain outcome |
| @vazquez2021 | Guayule/guar supply-chain design with sustainability criteria | Processing yields and sustainability constraints change comparability |
| @mogale2020 | Multi-echelon grain network with risk and losses | Losses and discrete transport resources require additional balances |

: Selected agricultural network-design studies. {#tbl-literature}

## Parameters, decisions and objective functions

Economic formulations typically connect fixed facility choices to continuous material
flows. The opening variable controls whether infrastructure can be used, while
installed capacity determines how much can be stored or handled. A benchmark must
distinguish a fixed-size site choice from scalable capacity: both may contain a
binary opening variable, but their investment feasible sets differ. Counting
producing regions or candidate sites is not an integer decision variable unless the
optimizer actually selects that count. Agricultural models also differ in the
economic boundary. While some consider freight and construction alone, others include
freight, inventory, processing, emissions, losses and employment in the objective.
@mogale2020 include risk and post-harvest losses in a green food supply-chain design.
@vazquez2021 connect supply-chain design to environmental and social impacts;
@mogale2023 examine social sustainability. Those dimensions are relevant to public
planning but are outside the scope of the present formulation.

Logistics costs depend on more than distance. @kussano2012 analyze soybean export
logistics using a broader cost accounting boundary, including factors that can alter
the ranking of modal alternatives. Accordingly, road-network distances associate
freight approximation based on modeled loads and unit transport costs. Congestion,
taxes, service contracts and seasonally changing tariffs remain possible sources of
divergence between the least-cost modeled route and actual grain movements. Spatial
suitability and network optimization are complementary rather than substitutable.
@souza2024 use spatial multicriteria analysis for agricultural warehouse location;
such screening can constrain the candidate set before a flow model allocates
capacity. The present candidate population preserves geographic and facility-type
diversity but does not replace environmental, land-use or engineering suitability
assessment. Similarly, the wider agricultural and carbon implications of Brazilian
transport infrastructure examined by @wang2024 lie outside a freight-and-storage
objective. A shorter modeled route cannot be interpreted automatically as a net
environmental gain.

## Uncertainty and strategic interpretation

Uncertainty can enter a model through simulation, scenarios, robust constraints or
probabilistic objectives. These approaches answer different questions. @granillo2019
combine a deterministic optimization model with simulation in a barley
contract-farming network. @mendoza2021 study scenario-based facility location, while
the adoption scenarios in @vazquez2021 concern a different source of uncertainty.
@pourmohammadi2020 provide a closer stochastic infrastructure precedent: six
equiprobable supply-demand scenarios, shared choices among four facility-capacity
levels, and scenario-dependent operation. Their assumptions prohibit shortage and
include imports, quality blending and road/rail transport. The present research
instead sizes capacity continuously, represents road movements and permits penalized
shortages. These differences change the feasible set and the meaning of optimal cost
outcomes. @maiyar2019 model emergency hubs as physical options for disruptions. The
slacks used in the present study quantify excess demand on nominal capacity within
the modeled network. Integrated decision support links planning horizons and
optimization [@mardaneh2021]. The joint crop-establishment, harvesting and
network-design perspective of @anselmino2025 provides another example, in bioenergy
rather than grain storage. Such work motivates clear interfaces between data
preparation, strategic investment and network evaluation.

## Computational approaches in agricultural systems

@shastri2011 address a large agricultural optimization model through a decomposition
and distributed-computing approach to BioFeed, a biomass supply planning problem.
This is direct precedent for treating computational solution strategy, rather than
the use of a commercial optimizer alone, as a research contribution. @knapen2025 use
standard big-data and distributed-computing technologies for scalable crop-growth
simulations. Their application illustrates a different parallelization opportunity:
distributing simulation work is not equivalent to solving a MILP whose scenarios
share first-stage integer decisions. @zhao2012 study parallelization and optimization
of spatial analysis for environmental model-data assembly. This distinction supports
measuring data preparation separately from the numerical solver rather than
attributing all elapsed time to optimization. @tbl-computational-literature relates
the agricultural planning problem to computational approaches at the optimization,
simulation and data-processing levels.

| Computational layer | Published precedent | Present implementation and evidence boundary |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Agricultural MILP solution strategy | @shastri2011 | Direct extensive-form solution; decomposition is not implemented in the evaluated scalar pipeline |
| Distributed agricultural simulation | @knapen2025 | Slurm experiment scheduling, not a distributed scenario solver |
| Spatial data preparation | @zhao2012 | Versioned OSRM materialization and pair-cache reuse; no matched speedup benchmark |

: Computational approaches for agricultural planning. {#tbl-computational-literature}

# Materials and methods

The investment formulation follows @rosa2026thesis in its treatment of facility
opening, expansion and bulk-handling conversion. Bulk-handling conversion is usually
implemented with additional equipment and process improvements rather than capacity
expansion. The objective function accounts for investments once and weights recourse
costs by scenario probability. Investment decisions are shared across scenarios, and
each scenario has a separate operating trajectory [@birge2011].

{{< include formulation.qmd >}}

## Data lineage and network construction

The study examines one grain-storage network design problem at four instance
sizes. The instances share supply and demand data, a 60-period planning
horizon, scenario inputs, model parameters and the tables of freight,
storage and investment costs. All four retain the same 146 existing
warehouses. Each larger instance adds candidate locations where a new
warehouse may be opened and retains the candidates of the smaller instance.
@tbl-warehouse-populations shows how the sets expand.

| Instance | Existing warehouses | Candidate locations | Total sites |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| h215 | 146 | 69 | 215 |
| h300 | 146 | 154 | 300 |
| h400 | 146 | 254 | 400 |
| h500 | 146 | 354 | 500 |

: Warehouse populations in the four processed inputs. {#tbl-warehouse-populations}

Each processed input workbook combines the common data with the warehouse
list and directed road distances for one instance. A facility identifier
distinguishes warehouses, including those that share coordinates. The
selection record lists the facilities in the instance and records the
stratified ranking used to add candidates. The optimizer chooses which of
the available sites to open, expand or convert to bulk handling. Appendix D
identifies the four effective workbooks, their warehouse lists and the
source data used to construct them.

The inputs include 37 distinct supply-location identifiers for soybean and
corn, 27 domestic-capital destinations and ten export-destination roles.
A city may hold both a domestic and an export role. The processed workbooks
store 63,289, 113,269, 190,569 and 287,869 directed road distances in
kilometres for h215, h300, h400 and h500, respectively. OSRM computed the
distances from a common Brazilian OpenStreetMap extract and driving profile.
The model uses a subset of routes eligible for each product. As candidates
are added, the set of admissible arcs and the dimensions of the MILP can
change. Appendix D documents the distance calculation and arc selection.

DET uses the original supply and demand arrays. STO crosses three supply
levels (0.85, 1 and 1.15 times the base supply) with three domestic-demand
levels (0.95, 1 and 1.05 times the base demand). Each of the nine resulting
scenarios has probability 1/9. The objective measures an undiscounted BRL
total over the 60 periods.

## Experimental and validation protocol

For each instance, the model selects warehouse openings and expansions, assigns
capacity and plans the movement and storage of grain. The study reports investment,
transport and inventory-holding costs. Unmet demand and the two capacity exceedances
are used to assess how closely the returned plan meets the modeled operating
conditions.

The h215 case provides the reference scale for comparison with the formulation of
@rosa2026thesis. It crosses DET and STO with two network configurations. W routes
grain through warehouses; D also permits direct origin-to-customer deliveries. Two
solvers are implemented in this study: a commercial solver (Gurobi[^author-1]), with
a native implementation and a Pyomo[^author-2] integration; and an open-source solver
(HiGHS[^author-3]) only with a Pyomo implementation. The native Gurobi comparisons
use four solver threads. The h215 W STO runs through Pyomo provide a separate
Gurobi-HiGHS comparison with the settings in Appendix C.

The native implementation builds and solves the model directly with
gurobipy[^author-4]. The native scale comparison uses W STO at h215, h300, h400 and
h500. The h300 experiment includes one observation at each of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16
threads, and the larger native cases have one thread each. The common-Pyomo campaign
applies one experimental design to h300, h400 and h500 W STO: two solvers, five
thread ceilings and three repetitions per combination, with seed 42, an eight-hour
native time limit and a 1% gap target. Pyomo builds the model once per run and passes
the same algebra for a given instance through the automatic persistent Pyomo solver
interface (APPSI[^author-5]) to Gurobi or HiGHS. Appendix C records the settings and
outcome coverage for each experiment.

An independent check reconstructs costs and tests the exported decisions
in their original units. It uses an absolute tolerance of $10^{-5}$ and a
relative tolerance of $10^{-8}$ scaled to the quantities compared.
For minimization, the common relative gap is $(z-b)/|z|$ for finite
nonzero incumbent objective $z$ and finite lower bound $b\le z$. The gap
is zero if both values are zero. It is unavailable for other zero
incumbents, missing or nonfinite values, or inconsistent bounds.
The gap measures the quality of the objective that includes the penalties.

## Solver parallelism and reproducibility

The common-Pyomo campaign sets the solver thread ceiling to 1, 2, 4, 8
or 16. Gurobi uses one MIP search (`ConcurrentMIP=1`) with parallel
algorithms that can use the specified threads. HiGHS 1.15.1 uses
`parallel="on"` to enable parallel tree search within its thread ceiling.
In that version, the simplex solver used for the LP relaxations inside
the MIP runs serially. The computational effect of extra threads
therefore depends on where each solver spends its time.

In branch-and-bound, the solver chooses a subproblem to explore, solves
its relaxation and uses the resulting bound and candidate solutions to
guide the next steps. The seed fixes the initialization of a solver's
pseudo-random choices. Branching, node selection, cuts and heuristics
also depend on the evolving search state. Thread settings can change
that state and the resulting trajectory. A time limit can stop repeated
runs at different points in their search. Appendix C explains the two
parallel modes, the settings used and how to interpret the repetitions.

## HPC experimental environment

The high-performance computing (HPC) experiments use NPAD/UFRN's Intel shared-memory
infrastructure under Slurm [@npad2026]. Retained runtime receipts identify Intel Xeon
E5-2698 v3 CPUs, Python 3.13 and Gurobi 13.0.3. The scalar allocations request 24
logical CPUs and 192 GiB. Gurobi's SoftMemLimit is 160 GB, but this is not a
process-RSS ceiling. The historical native h300 worker affinity pool contains 16
logical CPU IDs across 12 physical cores, including SMT siblings. Solver threads,
affinity and allocated logical CPUs are distinct registered resource scopes.

For the common-Pyomo campaign the profile requests an exclusive node and
192 GiB for a 12-hour allocation. The h300 worker affinity is 16 logical
CPU IDs. Scheduler accounting records 64 allocated logical CPUs at the
job level for the scientific jobs. Solver thread ceilings are settings within
this envelope. The runtime and hardware receipts identify the conditions
for each numerical observation.

Historical native reservations are 14 hours for the h215 pair, 30 hours for the
five-arm h300 block, and eight hours each for h400 and h500. Reservation time is not
measured optimizer time. Current models solve within one allocated node, and the
reported scalar blocks run serially. Distributing independent experiments through
scheduler arrays could not make an individual model a distributed MILP solve; no
multi-node speedup has been claimed. Network preparation, construction and
post-processing are CPU workloads outside the primary optimization call. No GPU
acceleration or use of the InfiniBand fabric by a distributed MILP algorithm was
asserted.

## Model size, memory and performance measurement

With retained product-eligible arcs $\mathcal A_p$, flow variables grow as
$|S||T|\sum_p|\mathcal A_p|$. Inventory contributes terms proportional to
$|S||T||W||P|$, with separate slack and first-stage blocks. Before screening,
the directed interwarehouse graph can contain $|W|(|W|-1)$ arcs. A fixed retained
fraction therefore does not eliminate quadratic network growth. These are
structural matrix counts, not an asymptotic algorithmic-complexity proof.

The native runtime, model-construction wall time, application optimization wall time,
extraction, validation, export and application end-to-end time are separate clocks.
Allocation elapsed includes additional staging and control. The microsecond data-read
fields at an already-loaded model layer are not large-workbook ETL timings. The study
does not reconstruct missing phases by subtracting overlapping clocks. Memory labels
distinguish sampled application RSS, solver-managed memory and Slurm step MaxRSS.
Sampling may miss an instantaneous peak; requested memory and allocated CPU-hour
products are not measured consumption or billing.

For a fixed instance and solver, strong scaling varies resources while
holding the problem fixed. With comparable work, timing and quality
criteria, speedup is $S(p)=T(1)/T(p)$ and parallel efficiency is
$E(p)=S(p)/p$ for a $p$-fold resource setting relative to the baseline.
In this study a ratio normalized by the configured thread ceiling measures
performance relative to that setting. Effective CPU utilization requires
a separate measurement. A time-to-target comparison uses the recorded time
when a common quality threshold is first attained. Terminal runtime also
includes work up to the observed stopping condition.

Across populations the experiment evaluates problem-size and resource
scaling. The selected graph and the number of nonzeros change
nonproportionally, while classical weak scaling keeps the workload per
resource approximately constant. Nonzeros per thread describe structural
load. Solver parallelism concerns work within one solve. Concurrent Slurm
jobs concern independent executions. Throughput would count specified
completed work per unit elapsed time over a stated allocation and
observation window.

# Discussion

## What scales with the planning problem

The h215 results show the cost of introducing scenario-dependent
operation while retaining the same shared investment binaries. The
near-ninefold expansion in variables and nonzeros accompanies a
twentyfold increase in the observed native time. Matrix size gives a
direct measure of formulation size and helps explain storage and build
requirements. Search and LP work also depend on the coefficients,
bounds, incumbent path and attained stopping gap.

In the native one-thread STO series, the increasing build times and
RSS from h300 to h500 are directly relevant to sizing a workstation
or HPC allocation. The higher effort buys a different planning
choice set, with additional candidate sites and different admissible
routes. Population, arcs and available decisions change jointly.
This is problem-size scale-up. Classical weak scaling would require a
design that maintains approximately constant workload per resource.

## Thread ceilings, terminal effort and usable plans

The common-Pyomo h300 block shows why a solver thread setting should be
evaluated jointly with the quality of the returned solution. The
Gurobi comparison has complete target attainment and closely aligned
attained gaps across the five settings. One thread delivered the
lowest median time on both clocks, with less sampled memory than the
higher settings. The gap between native and end-to-end ratios matters
for practitioners who need a validated investment report. Build,
transfer and checking contribute to that elapsed time. The observations
measure neither CPU utilization nor a causal allocation of time to
parallel overhead.

At one thread both solvers delivered usable h300 plans. At the higher
ceilings, HiGHS returned only a bound within the observed budget.
Treating those terminal times as times to solution would reverse the
scientific meaning of the comparison. The useful result is the observed
attainment contrast at a fixed size, together with the bound,
termination state and resource use. These fixed-seed repetitions
characterize variability on the same instance and protocol. They do
not sample independent planning problems or establish a general solver
ranking.

The h400 pilot comparison adds an operational constraint. An accepted
incumbent can coexist with insufficient memory reserve for progression.
The original 16-thread Gurobi pilot satisfied the numerical target and
exceeded the progression gate's sampled-peak ceiling. A study that
reports only accepted gaps would miss this distinction. The subsequent
h400 runs use separate receipts and monitoring and are documented as
such in Appendix C. Reliable comparisons across these runs depend on
the resource profile and complete validation records.

## Implications for grain-storage investment

The native W STO plans show a shift in expenditure as the candidate
set grows. From h215 to h500, the returned one-time investment increases
from BRL 9.82 billion to 14.32 billion while transport decreases from
BRL 367.14 billion to 346.07 billion. The economic subtotal falls from
BRL 393.90 billion to 373.17 billion. Installed candidate capacity
increases from 7.38 to 10.99 million tonnes. The h500 incumbent allocates
capacity across all 354 candidate locations. That distribution reflects
the encoded costs, routing and service trade-offs and would require
site-level validation before implementation.

The h215 W/D results illustrate why economic expenditure and service
should be read together. With direct deliveries, the returned D plans
have economic subtotals 13.11% lower in DET and 13.66% lower in STO.
Domestic service falls by 1.97 and 2.41 percentage points, respectively.
Direct deliveries bypass some warehouse handling and stock, while the
optimization trades off shortage and capacity penalties under the same
weights. In the native W STO series, service also varies nonmonotonically
as the candidate set expands. Lower expenditure alone is therefore an
incomplete basis for selecting an investment program.

Artificial penalties represent roughly 94–97% of the native W/D
penalized objectives. A certified gap applies to the penalized total.
The economic subtotal, delivered grain and the three physical slack
measures remain separate. A planner can use those diagnostics to
identify where a returned investment plan depends on unmet demand or
capacity exceedance. Stock summed over time is measured in
tonne-periods, whereas reception overflow is measured in tonnes.

The first common-Pyomo h300 pair further shows how similar aggregate
outcomes can hide different investments. Both solutions open the same
154 candidates and report domestic service close to 91.33%. They
share 69 expansion sites and 76 bulk-handling sites. The Gurobi plan
adds one expansion to the shared set. The HiGHS plan adds one
bulk-handling conversion to the shared set.
Appendix E retains the individual facility identifiers, capacities and
directed flows, which are the evidence needed to identify decisions
that are consistent between the two plans.

## Relationship to agricultural computing research

The evidence complements the tactical effort measurements of @reis2023
by linking construction, solver effort and memory to long-lived
warehouse investment. The discrete sizing and demand fulfillment in
@pourmohammadi2020 frame the different implications of continuous sizing
and penalized domestic shortage here. The capacity-relief mechanism
in @milanez2026 motivates reporting operational quantities alongside
the numerical certificate. The distributed decomposition in
@shastri2011 addresses a related computational burden using a different
solution strategy. The present measurements characterize direct
extensive-form solution under declared configurations and supply
a reproducible comparison within the study.

The complementary human-supervised workflow links each computational
claim to an input, execution and validation record. Appendix B
describes the decisions and checks that make this evidence traceable.
The primary contribution remains the joint characterization of
computational requirements and grain-storage decisions.

# Final considerations, limitations and future work

Eleven validated native Gurobi observations met the 1% gap target.
The native W STO series reached 63.43 million variables and 244.04
million nonzeros at h500. Its returned plan assigns capacity to 354
candidate sites, expands 72 existing warehouses and converts 74 for
bulk handling. The attained gap is 0.207432% and modeled domestic
service is 91.636%. The reported investment, costs and physical
diagnostics make the planning trade-offs inspectable.

Gurobi and HiGHS returned independently validated Pyomo plans for h215
W STO and for the first matched h300 W STO pair. Across the complete
h300 repetition grid, Gurobi met the target in 15 of 15 runs and HiGHS
in three of 15. The Gurobi one-thread median was lowest on both timing
clocks. At 16 threads the nominal native efficiency was 3.1% relative
to the one-thread baseline. These indicators describe a fixed-instance
comparison with the declared options and gap policy. The h400 evidence
is at pilot scale and the h500 computational result comes from the
historical native implementation.

The main limitations are the fixed sets of instances and scenarios,
three temporal repetitions per repeated setting, finite compute
budgets and incomplete coverage at the larger sizes. The investment
conclusions also depend on the represented sites, costs, period
structure and penalties. Decision support for implementation requires
credible local costs, site suitability and explicit service
requirements.

## Future work

Use the completed h400 qualification pilots and the final verified E2
receipts to assess coverage of the five thread settings under the 192 GiB
profile. Quantify repeated h400 performance when comparable observations
are available. Progression to h500 depends on a separate resource
qualification. Retain the matrix, stopping, timing and memory identities
needed for each comparison, as specified in Appendix C.

A separate planning study could test calibrated costs and service
requirements. That comparison would evaluate how the resulting
investments change relative to the present plans.

# Reproducibility and availability

The source code, experiment definitions and numerical records are available in
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic). Each
experimental record identifies the source version, input, warehouse population,
settings, decisions and original validation. A later integrity check does not change
the identities of the executed software or its results.

The article and supplementary material are written in Quarto[^author-6] and can be
rendered without an optimizer or HPC credentials. Appendix A presents the literature
review; Appendix B explains AI-assisted research and verification; Appendix C
describes the Python implementations, independent validation and GAMS[^author-7]
translation; Appendix D specifies input data and effective parameters. GAMS
compilation and numerical parity have not been verified. The Python results therefore
do not constitute numerical validation of that translation.

The supplementary material is accessible as
[HTML](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/supplementary-review.html)
and [PDF](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/supplementary-review.pdf).
Exact source snapshots and data identities are given in the linked repository.

The editable [article TeX](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/index.tex)
and [appendix TeX](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/supplementary-review.tex)
are generated from the Quarto sources. Their figures, bibliography, class files
and notices accompany the [complete editable project](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/editable-sources.zip).
The individual TeX downloads are intended for editing; compilation requires
those accompanying dependencies.

## Data availability

The research dataset is publicly available in Zenodo, version 0.2.0
[@celestino2026dataset], at
[10.5281/zenodo.22751909](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22751909).
The [processed input archive](https://zenodo.org/records/22751909/files/agrologistic-v020-inputs.zip?download=1)
contains the four effective workbooks. Appendix D lists the exact members
and checksums for h215, h300, h400 and h500. Appendices D and E identify
the decision vectors and flow-distance companions and explain how to
access them. OpenStreetMap derivatives retain ODbL terms, and
project-authored code is MIT. File-level access and redistribution
conditions are recorded in the dataset inventories.
